citation: Mülkoğlu C, Nacır B. Notalgia paresthetica: clinical features, radiological evaluation, and a novel therapeutic option. BMC Neurol 2020;20(1):191
text_quality: ok (born-digital PDF, 8 pages; text, Tables 1–3, figure legends and references 1–33 all extracted; Fig. 1–2 are clinical photographs with no data). Free full text also in PMC (PMC7229619).
design: Single-centre study that the authors call cross-sectional, with two parts: (1) a clinical and radiological comparison of notalgia paresthetica (NP) patients with dorsalgia patients without NP; (2) a non-randomised, unblinded, uncontrolled before-and-after treatment series of intradermal lidocaine in part of the NP group. How the treated NP patients were chosen is not stated. The other NP patients were prescribed topical capsaicin, but no outcomes are reported for them and the two treatments are not compared; the authors state they had no NP control group without lidocaine. PubMed indexes the paper as 'Clinical Trial' (MeSH 'Cross-Sectional Studies'). The title calls the treatment 'a novel therapeutic option'; the authors do not claim to be the first and cite their own earlier single-case report of local lidocaine injections in NP (ref 12, 2018). They frame the method as therapeutic local anaesthesia (neural therapy).
population: Adults seen in a physical medicine and rehabilitation outpatient clinic: 45 with notalgia paresthetica (39 women; mean age 54.7 years; pruritus in all, burning 49%, paresthesia 44%, hypoesthesia 40%, hyperpigmented patch 76%; median symptom duration 12 months) and 35 with dorsalgia without NP. Excluded: under 18, chronic inflammatory, infectious, neurological, psychiatric, rheumatologic or malignant disease, other skin disease, spinal trauma.
n: 80 in total: NP 45, dorsalgia comparison group 35 (radiological comparison only). Lidocaine treatment planned for 22 NP patients; 2 did not attend the second session and were excluded; 20 analysed. Remaining NP patients (about 23) prescribed topical capsaicin, not reported.
setting: Department of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, Health Sciences University Ankara Training and Research Hospital, Ankara, Turkey; patients presenting August 2018 to June 2019.
intervention: Intradermal injection of plain lidocaine diluted with saline [dose figure omitted], each injection raising a small bump (papule) in the skin, at pencil-marked points around the hyperpigmented patch and segmentally along and beside the C2–T6 spinous processes, patient prone; chlorhexidine-alcohol skin antisepsis. No vasoconstrictor or other additive is named. Needle gauge and injection depth are not stated. What the study did: three sessions, the first followed by repeats at weeks 2 and 4 (two-week intervals).
comparator: None for the treatment: no sham, saline, waiting-list or untreated NP group; the capsaicin-prescribed NP patients were neither reported nor compared. The 35 dorsalgia patients were a comparison group for the clinical and radiological findings only.
route: Intradermal (papules/wheals) in the skin of the upper back.
duration: Four-week treatment course; follow-up to 3 months from the first session (about 2 months after the last).
outcomes: VAS pain and VAS pruritus (0–10) at day 0, week 2, week 4 and 3 months (Table 3; Friedman's test); adverse effects noted at the week-2 and week-4 visits; spine X-ray and MRI findings (NP vs dorsalgia). NOT measured or reported: any sensory testing after the injections (pinprick, touch or thresholds), patient-reported numbness, onset or duration of skin anaesthesia, skin biopsy or nerve-fibre measures. The neurological examination 'for motor and sensorial functions' was done at enrolment only. Whether the week-2 and week-4 scores were taken before or after that visit's injection is not stated, and the results sentence ('After the third session ... decreased at the second- and fourthweek follow-up') does not fit the schedule, since the third session was at week 4.

key_results.quote: We also investigated the effect of intradermal lidocaine injection on patients with NP.
After the diagnosis of NP and physical examination, therapeutic lidocaine injections were planned for the 22 patients in the NP group.
Small bumps appeared on the skin.
Topical capsaicin was prescribed to the remaining patients in the NP group.
All of the patients were called for a follow-up at the second and fourth weeks and third month. The VAS-pain and VAS-pruritus scores were assessed at these visits.
We planned local lidocaine injections for 22 patients. Since 2 patients did not come to the second injection, they were excluded from the study and the evaluation … was made on 20 patients.
After the third session of lidocaine injection, the VAS-pain and VAS-pruritus scores were significantly decreased at the second- and fourthweek follow-up.
The median VAS-pain score 0.day 8 (5–9) 2nd week 4 (3–6) 4th week 2 (2–5) p < 0.001 After 3 months 2 (1–4)
The median VAS-pruritus score 0.day 7 (5–8) 2nd week 5 (3–6) 4th week 1 (0–4) p < 0.001 After 3 months 1 (0–3)
We did not observe any adverse effect due to lidocaine at the follow-up visits at the second and fourth weeks.
The relief of pain and pruritus continued for up to 3 months.

In the current study, 20 patients in the NP group suffering from pruritus and neuropathic pain were locally administered therapeutic lidocaine, and improvement was observed to sustain for up to 3 months.

We obtained successful results in relieving of pain and pruritus of the patients with NP by simple intradermal lidocaine injections. Therefore, we did not consider the need to block the dorsal spinal nerves with a deeper injection method.
Therapeutic local anesthesia (neural therapy) is a modality using injections with local anesthetics for diagnosis and therapy
The real purpose, though, is not to apply local anesthetics.

We also previously reported a 73-year-old male case with NP treated with therapeutic lidocaine injections. In that case, we locally administered lidocaine into the upper back to relieve pain and obtained successful results related to neuropathic back pain.
Hypoesthesia was present in 18 patients (40%) and hyperesthesia in three (7%)
There was a significantly higher number of HNP at the C6–7 segment and cervical degenerative changes in the NP group (p < 0.05).

author_limitations.quote: Firstly, the radiological findings of the patients were evaluated by X-ray and MRI, but their consistency with the clinical findings was not evaluated.
Secondly, the patients were not followed up after the third months of lidocaine application.
It remains unclear whether the efficacy of lidocaine treatment is durable or continuous injections are required for greater benefit in patients with NP.
We also did not have a control group with NP who did not undergo lidocaine treatment.
Thirdly, in the current cross-sectional study, it was difficult to draw definitive conclusions concerning the treatment applied.

funding_conflicts: Funding: 'Not applicable.' Competing interests: 'The authors declare that they have no competing interests.' (p7). Approved by the hospital's Clinical Research Ethics Committee; written informed consent. The same two authors (with a third) published the earlier single-case report of this treatment (ref 12, Int J Dermatol 2018).
